result.rationale: The diff adds refreshOAuthTokens whose comment documents the sync endpoint contract as returning 'only the access token and expiry date', while consumers parse the returned response with app-specific expectations: GoogleCalendarService reads token.expiry_date, HubSpot reads expires_in and computes expiry_date, Zoom uses parseRefreshTokenResponse (which also fabricates refresh_token='refresh_token'). If the sync response contains only access_token + expiry in some generic shape, these consumers would read undefined fields and write broken credentials — a plausible correctness defect in the newl

adjudication.rationale: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, parseRefreshTokenResponse() switches to minimumTokenResponseSchema (requires access_token plus at least one numeric field) regardless of the app-specific schema. This can break real refresh flows that don’t match that “access token + expiry number” shape. For example, SalesforceCalendarService now calls parseRefreshTokenResponse(accessTokenJson, salesforceTokenSchema), but Salesforce’s refresh response (as implied by the newly added salesforceTokenSchema: id/issued_at/instance_url/signature/access_token/scope/token_type) contains no numeric expiry field, so minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response) will fail and throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" whenever credential sharing + sync endpoint are enabled. More generally, the comment in refreshOAuthTokens ("response should only contain the access token and expiry date") conflicts with consumers that rely on other fields (e.g., Lark’s refresh_access_token / other provider-specific fields).
